analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by federal, state, and local law enforcement and ties federal policing grants to compliance.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2015 with 24 Senate cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make racial profiling illegal for every law enforcement agent in the country — federal, state, local, and tribal — defining it as relying on race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, gender, gender identity, or sexual orientation when deciding whom to stop, search, or investigate. People subjected to profiling could go to court for a legal order to stop it, and statistical evidence that stops fall disproportionately on a group would count as initial proof of a violation. Police departments would have to adopt anti-profiling policies, training, and complaint systems, and would have to certify compliance to keep receiving two major federal policing grant programs. It would also require uniform data collection on stops and searches, with annual public reports on disparities.
analysis.who_benefits: People who get stopped, searched, frisked, or investigated because of their race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, gender, gender identity, or sexual orientation — particularly residents of heavily policed minority neighborhoods, who would gain a federal legal remedy and a right to sue for a court order ending the practice. Communities would also gain access to published data on who their police stop and search.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement agent or agency from engaging in racial profiling, and lets the U.S. or an injured individual sue for declaratory or injunctive relief in state or federal court.

Makes statistical evidence that investigatory stops have a disparate impact on a protected group prima facie evidence of a violation, and lets prevailing plaintiffs recover attorney's fees and expert fees.
Requires federal law enforcement agencies to maintain policies banning profiling, train officers, collect data, and handle complaints, and to cease existing practices that permit profiling.

Conditions Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant and Cops on the Beat funding on a certification that state and local agencies maintain anti-profiling policies, with the Attorney General empowered to withhold grants for noncompliance.

Requires Attorney General regulations for standardized collection of stop and search data by race, ethnicity, national origin, gender, and religion, with annual public reports analyzing disparities, including hit rates for stops and searches.
Authorizes grants to law enforcement agencies for training, data-collection technology, and complaint or audit systems, with an equitable share reserved for small and rural agencies.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies bear the costs: writing and enforcing new policies, training officers, collecting and reporting stop data, operating complaint procedures, and defending against lawsuits brought under the new private right of action. Local governments that fail to comply could lose part of their Byrne and COPS grant money. Taxpayers fund the new grant programs and the Justice Department's data collection and reporting work — the bill authorizes 'such sums as are necessary.'

drawbacks.text: The definition of racial profiling is broad — it covers religion, gender, gender identity, and sexual orientation, and applies to immigration and customs enforcement, including workplace immigration investigations and inspections of entrants — so agencies could argue it constrains legitimate border, customs, and immigration enforcement.

The private right of action treats a statistical disparate impact as prima facie evidence of a violation, which could expose departments to litigation based on stop data alone even where officers acted on specific, lawful information.

Compliance is expensive: agencies would have to build data collection systems, run training, and operate administrative complaint or independent audit procedures, and jurisdictions found noncompliant could have federal policing grants withheld in whole or in part.
The bill authorizes 'such sums as are necessary' in new federal spending for grants, a data-collection demonstration project, and Justice Department reporting, with no offset.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give individuals a concrete federal remedy for a practice that today is largely policed only by local policy, and would create nationwide data showing which departments stop minority residents disproportionately. The real costs fall on police agencies in money and litigation exposure, and the grant-withholding provision means compliance is effectively mandatory for any locality that relies on Byrne or COPS funding. Reasonable objections center on breadth — the definition reaches immigration and customs work and turns statistics alone into initial proof — but the bill was never debated or amended, so none of these concerns ever got weighed on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced in April 2015 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Cardin introduced the End Racial Profiling Act of 2015 in the Senate on April 22, 2015, joined by 12 original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
24 senators cosponsored the bill — 23 Democrats and 1 Independent; no Republican cosponsored.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill never left the Judiciary Committee, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies are better off: no federal profiling ban, no mandated data collection or complaint systems, no certification requirement attached to Byrne and COPS grant money, and no new private right of action against them. People subjected to profiling gained nothing from the two-year session.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies; profiling ban never advanced

for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland; bill sponsor

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the backing of a quarter of the Senate.

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred on the day of introduction — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the two-year session.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 24 cosponsors was a Democrat or the chamber's Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Judiciary Committee never brought the bill up.

industries.note: The bill would ban profiling, require anti-profiling policies and officer training, mandate stop-and-search data collection, and condition Byrne and COPS grant money on certification, with grant withholding for noncompliance. It also creates a private right of action and lets prevailing plaintiffs recover attorney's fees, exposing departments to lawsuits over stop patterns.

industries.industry: Federal immigration and customs enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill's definition of law enforcement explicitly covers immigration and customs agents and lists immigration-related workplace investigations and extended inspections of entrants as covered activities, narrowing discretion in border and workplace enforcement.

industries.industry: Justice Department grant and training programs (Byrne JAG, COPS, Bureau of Justice Assistance)
industries.note: The bill authorizes new appropriations for best-practices grants, a $5 million stop-data demonstration project, and Justice Department data analysis and annual reporting, routing new funding through these programs.
